message.content: {"title":"The Squeeze Has Two Exits, and the Data Can't Yet Say Which","intro":"The article has argued that the gap between cooling inflation and a still-rising cost of living is real, measurable, and unlikely to close on its own. What remains open is whether that gap narrows because wages finally catch up, or because households absorb the cost by spending less and saving less. The signposts below are the ones that would tell us which is happening.","scenarios":[{"key":"wage_catchup","name":"Wages close the gap","role":"central","summary":"Real median household income keeps climbing and the cumulative price level stops outrunning it, so the perception gap narrows from the income side rather than the price side.","conditions":["Real median household income extends its run at the top of the retrieved window rather than slipping back, with the one-year change staying positive.","Core CPI and core PCE one-year changes keep drifting down toward the Fed's target while the index levels flatten rather than fall.","Consumer sentiment recovers from its recent low as households register that paychecks stretch further, even if prices never return to where they were."],"whyItMatters":"For a median household this is the benign path: the level of prices stays high, but the arithmetic of a paycheck finally works again, and the squeeze eases without anyone having to relearn how to budget. It matters most for renters and for households that have been trading down, since it is the group whose real income gains have been thinnest.","assets":[{ "asset":"Equities","effect":"If real income growth holds and inflation keeps cooling, the compression in real equity returns described earlier would have less reason to continue, though a lower-inflation, slower-growth mix can cut both ways for earnings." },{ "asset":"10-year Treasury","effect":"A sustained decline in core inflation would typically pull yields lower from the current {t10yYieldLatest}, which helps bondholders through price gains but cuts the income new buyers lock in." },{ "asset":"Housing","effect":"A mortgage rate that has already risen by {mortgageRateChg1y} over the past year would need to fall before affordability improves much, and this scenario does not by itself deliver that." }],"watch":["The next readings of {realMedianIncomeLatest} versus the {cpiCoreLatest} and {corePCELatest} levels, and whether the one-year changes keep moving in opposite directions in the helpful way.","Whether {consumerSentimentLatest} climbs back toward its recent high of {consumerSentimentHigh1y} rather than staying near the {consumerSentimentLow1y} low.","Whether {cpiCoreChg1y} and {corePCEChg1y} continue to fall while the index levels stop making new highs."],"uncertainties":["Real median income is annual data, so a turn in the wage picture would show up slowly and could be revised.","A single year of real income growth does not undo the five-year gap: core CPI is up {cpiCoreChg5y} against {realMedianIncomeChg5y} for real median income, and closing that requires many more good years.","Sentiment has stayed depressed through stretches of decent income data before, so an improvement in the numbers is not guaranteed to move it."]},{"key":"persistent_squeeze","name":"Sticky costs outlast the slowdown","role":"alternative","summary":"Headline inflation keeps moderating, but housing and medical costs keep rising faster than the broader index, so the level of prices keeps climbing and the perception gap widens even as the headline rate looks better.","conditions":["Owners' equivalent rent and medical services keep posting monthly increases that outpace the broader index, as they have recently.","Core CPI and core PCE one-year changes stall above target rather than continuing to fall.","Real median household income gives back some of its recent gain, as California's already has with a one-year change of {realIncomeCAChg1y}."],"whyItMatters":"This is the path the article's mechanism section leans toward, and it hits households with the least room to absorb it hardest: renters facing renewal increases, and anyone with recurring medical costs. It also keeps the saving rate near its current {srcPersonalSavingRate}, which limits how much households can put toward long-term wealth building.","assets":[{ "asset":"Equities","effect":"Real returns, already down {sp500RealReturnChg1y} over the past year, would have little room to recover if input costs and rates stay elevated, though nominal index levels can still rise." },{ "asset":"10-year Treasury","effect":"Sticky core inflation tends to keep yields near the top of their recent range rather than the {t10yYieldLow1y} low, which supports income for holders but pressures prices." },{ "asset":"Cash and saving","effect":"With the saving rate at {srcPersonalSavingRate}, households have little buffer, so any further cost increase comes out of discretionary spending rather than savings." }],"watch":["Whether {cpiCoreLatest} and {corePCELatest} keep setting new highs in the data while their one-year changes stall.","Whether {consumerSentimentLatest} stays near the {consumerSentimentLow1y} low even as headline inflation cools.","Whether the monthly core increases quoted in recent releases, such as {srcCoreCpiMonthlyIncrease}, persist rather than fade."],"uncertainties":["The dataset does not break inflation down by category over the full five-year period, so the claim that housing and medical care are the persistent drivers rests on recent monthly data rather than a long-run decomposition.","Base effects can flatter the headline rate for a stretch without any real improvement in underlying costs, which would make this path look better than it is before it looks worse."]},{"key":"demand_break","name":"Households pull back hard enough to force the issue","role":"alternative","summary":"The trading-down behaviour described earlier accelerates into a broad pullback in discretionary spending, which cools prices faster than expected but at the cost of weaker growth and weaker income.","conditions":["Consumer sentiment stays depressed and households cut discretionary purchases further rather than merely trading down.","Retail and services demand soften enough that core services inflation falls faster than the current trend.","Real median household income growth slows or turns negative as the pullback feeds back into hiring and hours."],"whyItMatters":"This is the path the article's argument does not predict, because it closes the gap by shrinking demand rather than by raising incomes. It matters most for households whose income depends on discretionary spending, and for anyone counting on wage gains to repair their budget.","assets":[{ "asset":"Equities","effect":"A demand-led disinflation would likely hit earnings first, and the equity real return, already the lowest in the past year at {sp500RealReturnLatest}, would have further to fall before it recovers." },{ "asset":"10-year Treasury","effect":"Weaker growth typically pulls yields down from {t10yYieldLatest}, which helps bondholders through price gains even as the income on new purchases falls." },{ "asset":"Housing","effect":"Softer demand could ease rent growth, but a weaker job market would undercut the incomes that service a mortgage at {mortgageRateLatest}." }],"watch":["Whether {consumerSentimentLatest} falls back toward {consumerSentimentLow1y} rather than recovering.","Whether {realMedianIncomeChg1y} turns negative in the next annual reading.","Whether core services inflation falls faster than the recent monthly pace quoted in {srcCoreCpiMonthlyIncrease} suggests."],"uncertainties":["The dataset has no historical saving-rate series, only the current {srcPersonalSavingRate}, so a spending pullback would be hard to see in these indicators until it shows up in income and sentiment.","A demand-led slowdown and a supply-led improvement in inflation can look similar in the headline rate for months, which makes this path easy to misread early."]}] ,"attention":{"required":true,"reasons":["No fact tokens cover bond real returns, so the fixed-income discussion is framed qualitatively rather than with a real-return figure.","No historical saving-rate series is available, so the saving-behaviour path rests on the single current reading from S2.","Category-level inflation data is only recent, not five-year, so the housing and medical persistence claim is supported by recent monthly data rather than a long-run breakdown."]}}
